title: Economist Steve Hanke Says His Best Investment Is a Swiss Watch
summary:
A pocket watch and a parcel of farmland.
Veteran trader Steve Hanke counts those two items among the best investments and biggest misses of his life.
The hitsAt age 16, Hanke purchased a Patek Philippe pocket watch for $90 at an auction in Omaha.
Hanke now only wears the watch on special occasions, but "the rest of the time I admire it," he said.
The lessonHanke's pocket watch showcases the value of a storied brand, a good deal, a decadeslong holding period, and a beautiful object that can be worn and admired.

title: A market sell-off and a career-changing call: Inside Jake Woodson's first day as a Goldman partner
summary:
Thursday, November 5, was among Jake Woodson's more chaotic days as a trader at Goldman Sachs.
His mom joined Woodson and Goldman's larger credit business that evening in the private room of Monk McGinn's, a pub near the office.
How he got thereWoodson didn't always expect to end up at Goldman, even though he studied finance in college.
"If you were a betting person, you probably wouldn't bet that there would be a Goldman partner coming from that suburb," Woodson said.
He was a distressed credit trader during the pandemic, and, as the head of US distressed credit trading, steered his team through the 2023 banking crisis, before becoming the head of leveraged finance trading this fall.

title: Zambia’s copper boom attracts billions in investment, but who benefits?
summary:
Share Zambia’s copper boom attracts billions in investment, but who benefits?
on social mediaLusaka, Zambia – Zambia is attracting billions of dollars in mining investment as it seeks to become a significant supplier of minerals critical to the global energy transition.
President Hakainde Hichilema said more than $12bn had been invested in Zambia’s mining sector since 2022, as the government pushes to increase copper production and attract new investors.
The government has set an ambitious target of increasing annual copper production to 3 million tonnes by 2031, from less than 1 million tonnes in recent years.
Eugene Mulenga, a human rights defender, fears the government’s drive to increase mineral production could place enormous pressure on the environment.
